name: Gambler's fallacy
aliases: Fallacy of the maturity of chances
statement: After a run of one outcome in an independent chance process, people expect the other outcome next, as though a fair coin owed them a correction.
meaning: The process has no memory and the fallacy is the belief that it does. A wheel that has shown red six times is as likely to show red on the seventh spin as it ever was. Tversky and Kahneman filed the error under representativeness, which has its own entry, no. 145: people treat a short run as though it had to look like the long-run average, so a sequence that has strayed is expected to come back. Their 1971 paper states it directly. Subjects act as if every segment of a random sequence must reflect the true proportion, and if the sequence has strayed, a corrective bias in the other direction is expected. The claim is confined to independent events. Where draws are made without replacement, expecting a reversal is correct arithmetic rather than a bias. Laplace drew that line in the same paragraph in which he described the error.

origin.note: Laplace describes the error in the chapter translated as "Concerning Illusions in the Estimation of Probabilities". Dating it is awkward. Miller and Gelman report that Laplace's first full presentation of that chapter came in the fourth edition of 1819, and they quote it from the 1825 fifth edition, while Croson and Sundali date the first published account to Laplace (1820). The essay itself first appeared in 1814. Neither priority claim is flat: Croson and Sundali write that the first published account is Laplace's, Miller and Gelman write that it is the first they have seen, and Miller and Gelman name d'Alembert, who argued that tails was likelier after three heads, as the case that may have prompted Laplace's explanation. The representativeness account comes much later, from Tversky and Kahneman in 1971, who treated the name as already current and wrote that the pattern "has been called the gambler's fallacy".

evidence: Laplace was writing about people he had watched. Punters in the French state lottery, he reports, piled stakes on numbers that had not come up for a long time, judging that such a number ought to be drawn in preference to others. In the same chapter he describes men who wanted sons and who heard of a month full of boys with anxiety, imagining that the ratio of births had to balance by month's end and that girls were therefore due. His diagnosis was that people are carried back involuntarily to the origin of events. He also entered a caveat that later writers usually drop. A long run of heads is weak evidence that the coin favours heads, so the past is not always uninformative. Drawing a white ball from an urn holding limited numbers of white and black balls does raise the chance of a black one next, and Laplace writes that this ceases to hold once the urn is unlimited, which is the case the births have to be compared with. Clotfelter and Cook put the claim to a field test in 1993 using the Maryland daily numbers game. Money bet on a particular number falls sharply as soon as that number is drawn, then recovers to its former level over the course of several months.

replication.headline: Betting against a streak turns up again in roulette, in lotteries, in asylum courts and in baseball, and the opposite bias turns up in a casino game with 18 million hands.
replication.detail: Croson and Sundali coded 18 hours of security videotape from a Reno casino: 904 spins, 139 players, 24,131 bets. Of 531 even-money outside bets placed after at least one spin, 255 (48%) went against the previous outcome and 276 (52%) went with it, which is nothing. Binomial tests find no difference after streaks of one, two, three or four. After streaks of five the difference reaches p < .05, after six or more p < .01, and at six or more, 85% of bets are against the streak. Chen, Moskowitz and Shue found negative autocorrelation in three settings where decisions matter. Their asylum data covers 150,357 decisions by 357 judges across 45 courthouses, which is a count of rulings and not of applicants. A judge who granted the previous application was 0.5 percentage points less likely to grant the current one. That rises to 3.3 points among moderate judges deciding same-day cases of the same defensive status. A streak of two grants cut the grant rate by 5.5 points against a streak of two denials. Their loan officers are a framed field experiment in India, 188 officers across 1,528 sessions of six files each, with 7,640 observations in the baseline regression. Approving the previous loan cut the chance of approving the current one by 8 percentage points under flat incentives, and the coefficients under the two stronger incentive schemes were -0.007 and +0.010. The test that the three differ gives p = .0695. Their baseball sample is about 1.5 million called pitches over 12,564 games and 127 home-plate umpires, drawn from about 3.5 million pitches thrown between 2008 and 2012. A called strike made the next called pitch 0.9 percentage points less likely to be called a strike, holding measured pitch location fixed. Suetens, Galbo-Jørgensen and Tyran tracked the Danish lotto over 28 weeks of 2005, with 25,807 identified players in the full sample, 17,318 who had two consecutive weeks and 8,224 who ever changed their numbers. Money staked on a number fell about 1.6% in the week after it was drawn in the full sample, and about 3.3% among the changers. The authors call the full-sample effect the weakest of the three and report it as marginal when the hotness term is left out. The same players moved towards numbers with longer recent runs, which is the hot hand rather than this fallacy. Barron and Leider showed the pattern depends on how the run arrives. Reversal appeared when outcomes were watched one at a time, with or without predictions in between, and was attenuated when the same outcomes were shown all at once. Xiang, Dorst and Gershman ran the tidiest laboratory test: five preregistered experiments of 150 Mechanical Turk workers each, 750 people in all, watching genuinely independent draws, with no participants or observations excluded. Asked to pick the next colour, participants chose reversal, with a posterior effect size of -0.51 and a 95% credible interval from -0.68 to -0.34 in Experiment 1b. Asked instead for the probability of the next colour, the same design produced nothing. Experiment 1a gave a median indistinguishable from 50%, Z = -1.03, p = .304. The posterior effect size was -0.11, with a credible interval from -0.27 to 0.05 and a Bayes factor of 0.248 favouring the null. Against all of that sits the largest field sample anyone has taken. Muto, Nakai, Murai, Yoshikawa and Abe analysed 17,970,830 baccarat games played by 6,625 customers at a land-based casino, and found bets moving with the streak rather than against it. Each extra step of streak length raised the odds of betting with the streak, β = 0.325, 95% CI 0.318 to 0.332, z = 89.31, p < .001 for player wins, and 91.5% of individual customers leaned that way. Kong, Granic, Lambert and Teo found the same split inside lottery play, with reversal in single-prize games and streak-following in games carrying two or three winning numbers. Rao and Hastie put six experiments to the question and found reversal only for a random mechanical device with a fixed base rate of one half.

study.cite: Chen, D. L., Moskowitz, T. J., & Shue, K. (2016). Decision making under the gambler's fallacy: Evidence from asylum judges, loan officers, and baseball umpires. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 131(3), 1181-1242. The n below counts asylum decisions, not judges and not applicants.

limits: No meta-analysis of the gambler's fallacy was located. Searches covered Crossref, Europe PMC, the Open Science Framework preprint index, arXiv and general web search, and returned individual studies and narrative reviews only, so the entry has no pooled estimate to quote and none should be inferred from the figures above. The field results carry caveats their own authors state. Croson and Sundali find nothing at streaks of one to four, which is where most roulette hands live. They also note that almost every roulette bet carries the same expected value, minus 5.26% on a double-zero wheel, so this is a setting where a costless bias can survive. Chen, Moskowitz and Shue say they cannot completely rule out sequential contrast effects as an alternative to the gambler's fallacy, and the magnitudes quoted here were read from the February 2016 NBER working-paper version rather than the published article. The Danish lotto magnitudes were likewise read from the authors' working paper, not from the published article, and they are percentages of a small weekly stake rather than shifts in belief. Muto and colleagues do not claim the fallacy is absent everywhere. Their argument is that baccarat's structure and its scoreboard invite trend-following, and they treat the contrast with roulette as the result rather than a refutation of the earlier work. The Xiang result splits the claim in two, and the split is disputed. Betting against a streak replicates. Whether people also state a lower probability for the streak continuing is now argued over by people working from the same data. Banki and Simonsohn count responses instead of averaging them and report that after a streak of four, 57% of probability judgments call the streak overly likely to end against 31% that do the opposite. Choi and DeKay report that a fuller reanalysis yields strong evidence of the fallacy in those probability judgments and undermines the claimed gap between judgments and choices. A Crossref search in August 2026 finds both only as preprint deposits rather than peer-reviewed articles, and neither collected new data. Dorst argues that the reversal need not be irrational at all: Bayesians who start uncertain whether a process is streaky, and then watch data from one that is not, rule out streaky hypotheses faster than switchy ones, so the average one expects a switch. The retrospective gambler's fallacy, in which an observed streak makes people guess that a longer unseen sequence preceded it, is a claim about reconstructing the past rather than predicting the future. It has its own entry, no. 519, where the Many Labs 1 replication of Oppenheimer and Monin is reported, and it is not a replication of the classic fallacy.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating every expectation of reversal as irrational. Draws without replacement do make the unseen outcome likelier. A run of one outcome is evidence that the generator is biased towards it. Laplace made both points in the chapter on illusions, and the fallacy is specific to processes known to be independent and memoryless. The second error is calling the fallacy the inverse of the hot hand, entry no. 57. They are answers to different questions, one about outcomes and one about people. Croson and Sundali found both in the same 139 gamblers. Those gamblers bet against long streaks and also placed more bets after winning, 13.62 numbers on average after an inside win against 9.21 after a loss. The third is reading the field studies as measurements of belief. What the asylum, loan and umpire data show is negative autocorrelation in choices, and whether the same shift appears in stated probabilities is the live dispute over Xiang and colleagues' data. The fourth concerns the founding anecdote. Popular accounts have the ball at the Monte Carlo casino landing on black 26 times running on 18 August 1913, ruining gamblers who kept doubling on red. The English Wikipedia article rests the date, the count and the losses on a single citation, a BBC Future column by Tom Stafford dated 28 January 2015, and that column names no source of its own. No older record was obtained for this entry. Keyword searches of the Library of Congress Chronicling America newspaper collection for 1913 to 1916, of Crossref and of general web search returned modern retellings and nothing contemporary. The fallacy does not need the story.
